predecessors.name: Starčevo–Körös–Criș culture
predecessors.text: the Hungarian Alföld of the eastern (Alföld) Linear Pottery, "At around 5330 BC" to "until about 4940"

successors.name: Lengyel culture
successors.text: the middle Danube (5000 BCE) and the northern extent: Bohemia and central Poland (4500 BCE)

successors.name: Cucuteni–Trypillia culture
successors.text: the part of the Dniester extension that lies inside the Cucuteni-Trypillia culture's first shape (4800 BC): Moldova, Chernivtsi, Khmel'nyts'kyy, Ternopil', Vinnytsya

ledger.x: 5500 BCE: the Linear Pottery farmers, Europe's first great Neolithic culture, hold the middle Danube.
5300 BCE: the LBK spreads down the Rhine, Elbe, Oder and Vistula.
5330 BCE: the Alföld Linear Pottery takes the Hungarian plain from the Koros.
5200 BCE: the LBK reaches the Netherlands and the Paris Basin.
5200 BCE: the eastern extension to the Dniester.

5000 BCE: the Stroked pottery (Stichbandkeramik) phase, "5000-4500 BC", in which "lines of punctures are substituted for the incised lines"; "a population collapse of 'enormous magnitude' after 5000 BC".
5000 BCE: the Lengyel culture takes the middle Danube.
4940 BCE: the Alföld Linear Pottery ends, "until about 4940"; the Tisza culture that follows has no dossier.
4800 BCE: the Dniester lands inside the Cucuteni-Trypillia culture's first shape pass to it (that dossier begins c.

4800 BCE: the rest of the Dniester extension (L'viv, Ivano-Frankivs'k, Volyn, Rivne) lies outside the Cucuteni-Trypillia culture's first shape (Moldova, Chernivtsi, Khmel'nyts'kyy, Ternopil', Vinnytsya, Romanian Moldavia) and goes to nobody; "The end of the Eastern Linear Pottery culture and the LBK is less certain"…

4500 BCE: Bohemia and central Poland (Kuyavia, Greater Poland), the Stroked pottery land, pass to the Lengyel culture, which draws them from 4500 BCE (its northern extent, phase IV "Jordanow" in Bohemia, Osłonki in Poland).
4500 BCE: the LBK and Stroked pottery end.

certainty.note: An archaeological culture drawn by modern units along the loess belt: every edge is soft.
